analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal education funding to any school that paddles or physically punishes students.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut off federal funding from schools that use paddling never got a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would withhold federal education money from any state or school district that allows staff to hit students as punishment, while paying states and districts to adopt positive behavior programs instead. Under the bill's findings, 19 states still allowed paddling in public schools, and Black students — 18% of the national student body — were 40% of the students physically punished [S3]. The bill was introduced in January 2019 and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never took it up [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Students in the 19 states that still permitted corporal punishment, especially Black students and students with disabilities, who were disciplined at disproportionate rates. The bill's findings cite hundreds of thousands of paddlings each year, with injuries ranging from bruising to hospitalization [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students in states that still allow paddling

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any state or local education agency that allows corporal punishment from receiving federal education funds, so schools must end paddling to keep Title I and other money [S2][S3].
Lets a local district that bans paddling apply directly to the Education Department for funds even if its state is blocked, so children are not punished for their state's policy [S3].

Authorizes three-year grants to help states and districts replace physical punishment with evidence-based positive behavior supports, and directs a national assessment of compliance and best practices [S2][S3].
Allows school staff to use the lightest reasonable restraint when a student's behavior poses an imminent danger of physical injury — the ban does not stop protecting people in a crisis [S3].

analysis.who_pays: School districts and states that continued to allow paddling would face losing federal education funds until they changed policy, and Congress would pay for the new grants and the national assessment [S3]. Taxpayers generally would fund the grant program [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Districts that paddle, plus federal grant costs

drawbacks.text: The enforcement tool is cutting off federal money, which in a paddling state could reduce the very school budgets that serve the students the bill is meant to protect; districts could lose funding before replacement programs are in place [S3].
The ban does not reach private schools that receive no federal funds or home schools, so a child's protection would still depend on where they attend school [S3].

Critics of federal funding conditions generally argue that Congress should not dictate local discipline policy through the power of the purse; no opponent is on the record in the provided record because no hearing or vote ever occurred [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending a practice that the bill's own findings tie to hundreds of thousands of paddlings a year and stark racial disparities — is large and the mechanism is a funding condition schools can cure by simply changing policy. The real risk is transition: a state that dug in would put its federal funds and its students in a bind, and the grants meant to ease that transition depend on appropriations Congress never made.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in January 2019, and the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Alcee Hastings introduced the Ending Corporal Punishment in Schools Act of 2019 on January 23, 2019, with five original co-introducers [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced [S5].
Fifteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: School districts and states that continued paddling students faced no federal consequence. Children in those states got no protection, and supporters got no vote at all — not even a roll call to be held accountable on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Schools that continued to paddle students

for.name: Rep. Alcee Hastings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on January 23, 2019

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral in January 2019 and never reported it out or scheduled action on it during the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat — 15 of 231 — and no Republican signed on; since no vote was ever held, the record shows only this one-sided written support [S4][S5].

industries.industry: School districts in states that permit paddling
industries.note: The bill would cut their federal education funds until they ended a disciplinary practice the bill's findings say is disproportionately used against Black students. Their interest in keeping paddling runs against students' physical safety [S3].
